nameStory: Desmodesmus denticulatus gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'chain-bound' and 'small teeth,' referring to how these tiny green algae link together in chains with tooth-like projections. Since this microscopic organism lacks a widely-used common name, scientists simply call it by its scientific name - though 'toothed chain algae' would be fitting!
description: Desmodesmus denticulatus is a microscopic freshwater green algae that you'll never see with the naked eye - it's only visible under a microscope. These single-celled organisms arrange themselves in groups of 4 to 8 cells that form small, flat colonies. Each individual cell is oval-shaped and contains bright green chloroplasts that help it photosynthesize, just like larger plants.

idTips.label: Colony arrangement
idTips.description: Cells are arranged in flat, rectangular groups of 4-8 cells that look like tiny green bricks stuck together when viewed under a microscope

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are oval to elliptical, with smooth, curved edges that fit neatly against neighboring cells

idTips.label: Spines and projections
idTips.description: Outer cells in the colony often have small spine-like projections or 'teeth' extending outward, giving the colony jagged edges

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright grass-green color due to chlorophyll, with cells appearing uniformly colored throughout

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Entire colonies are only 20-40 micrometers across - thousands could fit on a pinhead

habitat: This microscopic algae floats freely in the water column of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It thrives in nutrient-rich waters where it can access plenty of dissolved minerals and sunlight for photosynthesis. You're most likely to find it in the upper layers of water bodies where sunlight penetrates.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase, making this a good time to find them in water samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when colonies are most abundant and easiest to find in pond and lake samples due to warm temperatures and long days.
seasonality.fall: Populations may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, but colonies can still be found in protected water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Greatly reduced numbers, though some may persist in unfrozen water bodies or survive as dormant cells.

funFact: Despite being invisible to our eyes, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these tiny algae colonies, and together they produce a significant portion of the oxygen we breathe - some scientists estimate that microscopic algae like this produce up to 70% of Earth's oxygen!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's easily confused with other colonial green algae like Scenedesmus, but Desmodesmus colonies tend to be flatter and more rectangular, while Scenedesmus often forms more curved or twisted arrangements. Remember: Desmodesmus = 'definitely square' formations.
contextualKnowledge: This organism was once classified in the genus Scenedesmus, so you may find older references listing it under that name. The genus was split relatively recently as scientists used genetic tools to better understand relationships between these microscopic algae species.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Desmodesmus communis, D. denticulatus has more pronounced spines or teeth on the outer cells of its colonies. While D. communis tends to have smoother colony edges, D. denticulatus lives up to its 'toothed' name with more obvious projections. The colony shape is also typically more rectangular and rigid compared to other species in the genus.
